exercises.approach: Construct `Series(values = c(3, 7), unit = "ms")` and call `series_total(x)`. The generic dispatches on x and finds the method registered with `S7::method(series_total, Series)`.
exercises.why: The values are finite and the unit is one nonempty string, so the validator returns NULL and construction succeeds. The method sums 3 and 7 and names the result with the unit, giving c(ms = 10).
exercises.wrong: Computing `sum(x@values)` outside the generic. The number is right, but the unit name is lost, so a later comparison with a named total fails and the reader no longer knows the scale.

exercises.approach: Call `join_series(x, Series(values = 5, unit = "ms"))`. The generic dispatches on both arguments and the list(Series, Series) method checks units before building a new Series.
exercises.why: Both units are ms, so the values are concatenated in argument order as 3, 7 and 5, and the total is 15. x itself still holds 3 and 7, because the method returns a new object.
exercises.wrong: Passing a bare 5 as the second argument. No method is registered for a Series paired with a plain number, so S7 stops instead of guessing that 5 is in milliseconds.

exercises.approach: Create the generic with `S7::new_generic("series_count", "x")` and register `S7::method(series_count, Series) <- function(x) length(x@values)`.
exercises.why: The generic dispatches on x alone. S7 validates whenever a Series is constructed or a property is set, so the method can trust its input, and length returns the integer 3L for the joined series.
exercises.wrong: Returning `as.numeric(length(x@values))`. It prints 3, but the value is double, so `identical(series_count(y), 3L)` is FALSE and the stated integer contract is broken.

exercises.approach: End the S7 validator with `if (length(problems)) problems else NULL`, returning NULL when the object is valid and a character vector of problems otherwise.
exercises.why: S7 reads NULL as valid and any character result as a list of problems. The S4 validity function in r-022 returns TRUE on success, and the two conventions look alike but are not interchangeable.
exercises.wrong: Copying the S4 ending `else TRUE`. S7 stops with a message saying the validator must return NULL or a character, not <logical>, so construction fails for perfectly valid inputs such as 3 and 7 in ms.
exercises.verify: `Series(values = c(3, 7), unit = "ms")` returns a Series without error when the validator ends with `else NULL`.

exercises.approach: Run `x@unit <- character(0)` inside a handler expecting "nonempty string", then read `x@unit` again.
exercises.why: S7 runs the validator whenever a property is replaced. character(0) has the right class, but the validator rejects it, and because the assignment fails, x keeps its previous unit.
exercises.wrong: Assuming S7 behaves like the S4 class in r-022, where `@<-` skips validity. Skipping this test would leave the most important difference between the two systems unchecked.
exercises.verify: The handler returns a message containing "unit must be one nonempty string", and `x@unit` still returns "ms".

exercises.approach: Work with a Series through its S7 constructor, properties and generics, and write an explicit adapter when S4 code needs the same data.
exercises.why: `@` is shared syntax, but S7 resolves it through its own property system. S4 methods such as combine_measure from r-022 are registered for FormalMeasure, so they have no method for a Series.
exercises.wrong: Passing a Series to combine_measure because both objects answer `@values`. Dispatch fails, and if it did not, the S4 validity rules would never have been checked for this object.
exercises.verify: `S7::S7_inherits(x, Series)` returns TRUE, and `class(x)` shows "Series" and "S7_object", not FormalMeasure.
